title: Would you use LinkedIn to find love?
summary: LinkedIn is primarily used for professional networking and career development, but some people have discovered that it might also be a useful dating app.

image.caption: Some users on LinkedIn say they use the site to vet potential dates and even to meet romantic partners. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New
LinkedIn is primarily used for professional networking and career development, but some people have discovered that it might also be a useful dating app.
Survey says 1 in 8 have used it to meet a romantic partner
Savannah Giedroyc and Robert DeMichele had mutual friends when they started dating, but their love story didn't begin the way you'd expect.
Instead of approaching DeMichele through their social circle, the Toronto-based accountant decided to take matters into her own hands — and shoot her shot on LinkedIn.

"I decided to send him an invite and then he accepted. It's so cheesy, because he ended up viewing my profile," said Giedroyc. "So then I viewed his back so that he would get the alert that, like, I was also looking at his profile. Then about a month later, he actually messaged me back on Instagram, because we were mutual."
"He says if I didn't add him [on LinkedIn] and I didn't … clue into his profile, he would have never put two and two together."
Savannah Giedroyc and Robert DeMichele on their wedding day in Toronto in August 2026. (Submitted by Savannah Giedroyc)

LinkedIn is primarily used for professional networking and career development, and allows people in the job market to post their resumés and browse listings and gives employers an opportunity to potentially find hires. Many people also publish their thoughts on business trends on the site, although users have noticed an increased number of AI-generated posts.
Recently, it’s made headlines for misleading job postings that funnelled applicants to a multi-level marketing company that asked for money.
But amid a sea of job postings (both real and fake) and AI slop, could LinkedIn actually be an underrated dating app?
Could you find your soulmate on LinkedIn?
A way to find, research potential partners

A poll by Zety — a professional development site that provides resumé and cover letter building services — surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. employees and found one in eight people said they formed a romantic relationship that started on LinkedIn. Twenty-two per cent said they reached out to, or responded to, someone on LinkedIn with romantic intent.
Some say the app also shines in another way: one in five respondents admitted to using LinkedIn to research a potential romantic partner.
"You see, like, where they went to school, their job — it kind of answers some questions. If you have certain boxes that you want to tick, it's all listed there for you," said Giedroyc.

"I would be lying if I said I haven't done it," said Emily Durham, a Toronto-based recruiter and content creator. "Dating is such a personal experience. I've always just been interested to see what [potential partners are] interested in."

More people are moving away from traditional dating apps such as Tinder, Bumble and Hinge. The Harris Poll, a global market research firm, surveyed 2,177 Americans and found 56 per cent of respondents agree the app meetups are "cringe" and 72 per cent said these apps have made dating feel more "transactional" than "romantic."
Almost half of those surveyed said they find information on LinkedIn to be more trustworthy than on traditional dating apps. (Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images)
Meanwhile, 48 per cent of respondents to the Zety survey find information on LinkedIn to be more trustworthy compared to actual dating apps.
Advances must 'feel safe'
Durham cautions that these types of advances must be reciprocal, with respect and consent at the centre of it all.

"For many women, when we show up online to advance our careers, what we also get is an onslaught of romantic advancement and sexual harassment," said Durham. "I think it's really about understanding how to make [those approaches] happen in a way that they'll feel safe … in a situation where there is reciprocity and it's mutual."
Not everyone is up for LinkedIn becoming more personal. Sixty five per cent of respondents to the Zety survey said they believe using the site for dating could harm their reputation.
But proponents say LinkedIn could help you judge whether a potential love interest is a go-getter.
"I think career and ambition says a lot about someone," said Giedroyc. "It’s one of the most important factors of someone's life — you know, what they do in the day-to-day."
